title: Tumor-informed circulating tumor DNA stratifies recurrence risk and survival in anal squamous cell carcinoma

paper_content.abstract: Patients with anal squamous cell carcinoma (ASCC) who fail chemoradiation (CRT) have poor outcomes, underscoring the need for biomarkers to guide risk stratification. In a real-world two-center cohort of 84 adults with non-metastatic ASCC treated with curative-intent CRT, we prospectively evaluate a tumor-informed circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) assay (SignateraTM, Natera). Here we show that across 647 plasma specimens, ctDNA is positive at pre-treatment in 79% (61/77), including 89% (24/27) with stage III disease. End-of-treatment ctDNA positivity identifies patients with inferior one-year outcomes: 63% overall survival, 44% progression-free survival, and 39% locoregional failure. Conversely, patients who were ctDNA-negative at baseline or who cleared ctDNA during-treatment have 100% locoregional failure-free survival. During surveillance, ctDNA re-emergence precedes clinical or radiographic relapse in every case. These findings support the consideration of ctDNA as a dynamic, treatment-responsive biomarker warranting prospective validation for risk-adapted surveillance and adjuvant therapy in ASCC.
paper_content.introduction:
Anal squamous cell carcinoma (ASCC) is a human papillomavirus (HPV)–associated malignancy for which definitive-intent (chemo)radiation (CRT) remains the standard treatment for non-metastatic disease.1-3 Although CRT often achieves long-term control and sphincter preservation, up to six months of serial evaluations may be required to assess treatment response.4 This prolonged interval may delay the detection of treatment failure, limit the window for effective salvage therapy, and contribute to patient anxiety and uncertainty in management. For patients with persistent or recurrent locoregional disease, salvage abdominoperineal resection (APR) remains the primary treatment, but it is associated with poor disease-specific and recurrence-free survival.5,6 These limitations underscore the need for early, reliable biomarkers to identify high-risk patients during or shortly after CRT, when timely therapeutic intervention may still improve outcomes.

Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) has emerged as a promising, minimally invasive blood-based biomarker that enables dynamic monitoring of disease burden through the detection of tumor-specific mutations in plasma.7-11 Prior studies in ASCC have predominantly focused on HPV-directed ctDNA assays,12-20 but these approaches may lack sensitivity in patients with HPV-negative (~5-10% of patients with ASCC).21,22 Tumor-informed ctDNA assays, customized to each patient’s unique mutational profile, may offer a more sensitive and broadly applicable alternative, although their utility in ASCC has not been well established yet.23,24

In this multicenter, real-world cohort study, we evaluated a commercially available, personalized, tumor-informed ctDNA assay for its prognostic and surveillance utility in patients with ASCC undergoing definitive-intent CRT. We hypothesized that ctDNA kinetics at pre-treatment, during-treatment, and end-of-treatment would correlate with clinical outcomes and, if validated, could inform risk-adapted, personalized treatment strategies.
paper_content.results:
Patient, Tumor, and Treatment Characteristics
Of 88 consecutive patients with localized ASCC who underwent definitive-intent dose-painted intensity-modulated radiation therapy (DP-IMRT), 84 patients (95%) had sufficient tumor tissue from diagnostic biopsies for ctDNA testing and were included in the final cohort (Figure 1A). Whole-exome sequencing (WES) identified key mutations across this population (Figure 1B). Demographic and treatment characteristics are summarized in Table 1 and Supplementary Table 1. The median follow-up among survivors, measured from diagnosis, was 18 months (interquartile range [IQR], 11–26 months).

ctDNA Detection and Temporal Dynamics
Across all timepoints, 647 plasma specimens were analyzed for ctDNA testing using a personalized, tumor-informed multiplex polymerase chain reaction-next-generation sequencing (mPCR-NGS) assay (SignateraTM) (Figure 1C). Cell-free DNA (cfDNA) concentrations increased during CRT, but ctDNA detection remained unaffected (Figure 1D). At pre-treatment, 79% (61 of 77) of patients were ctDNA-positive, including 89% (24 of 27) with stage III disease. Pre-treatment ctDNA positivity was significantly associated with T3/T4 tumors (odds ratio [OR], 4.08; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.01–27.6; P=0.049) and node-positive disease (OR, 8.33; 95% CI, 2.19–41.5; P=0.001) (Supplementary Table 2). As treatment progressed, ctDNA levels generally declined, though levels remained higher at each timepoint among patients with more advanced clinical stage, compared to stage I (Supplementary Figure 1 and Supplementary Table 3). Median ctDNA levels at pre-treatment, mid-treatment, and end-of-treatment were 1.02 MTM/mL (interquartile range (IQR), 0.17-25.43), 0 MTM/mL (IQR, 0-0.46), and 0 MTM/mL (IQR, 0-0). Of the end-of-treatment samples, 6 were drawn in the final week of CRT (−7 to -1 days), 7 on the final day of CRT (0 day), and 60 after CRT completion (+1 to +42 days) (Figure 1C).

Treatment Failure Events
The clinical courses of the cohort, grouped by baseline stage and outcome, are shown in Figure 2. Twelve patients (14%) experienced treatment failure (including death without progression) including seven locoregional failures, four distant failures, and one death (Supplementary Figure 2). Of the seven patients with locoregional failure, three had local-only failure, two had nodal-only failure, and two had combined local-nodal failure. Among patients with locoregional recurrence, three underwent salvage APR, two received nonoperative salvage with re-irradiation, and two were deemed medically ineligible for salvage therapy and was managed with best supportive care. Five deaths occurred in the post-CRT follow-up period. Four were attributed to disease progression including three from distant metastatic disease and one from locoregional recurrence as the patient died from complications of the recurrent tumor. At the last available disease assessment prior to death, all four had positive ctDNA. One additional patient died without evidence of disease progression due to complications of COVID-19 and Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile) colitis.

Among the 12 patients with treatment failure or death, 11 (92%) had at least one high-risk feature (tumor >4 cm and/or nodal involvement). All patients completed their prescribed course of CRT without dose reductions or treatment breaks. In a competing-risks analysis, absence of mitomycin at CRT and HPV status were not associated with increased hazard of locoregional recurrence (Supplementary Table 4). In all cases, ctDNA positivity preceded clinical or radiographic evidence of recurrence (Supplementary Figure 2). Notably, all patients who were ctDNA-negative at baseline remained recurrence-free during follow-up, suggesting this subgroup may represent particularly favorable biology.

Overall Survival, Progression-Free Survival, and Locoregional Failure
Pre-treatment ctDNA-negative patients had an estimated one-year overall survival (OS) of 100% (95% CI, 100-100%), compared to 97% (95% CI, 92-100%) for those with ctDNA-positive status (Figure 3A). Stratified by during-treatment ctDNA status, one-year OS was 100% (95% CI, 100-100%) for ctDNA-negative versus 93% (95 % CI, 84-100%) for ctDNA-positive patients (Figure 3B). At end-of-treatment, ctDNA-negative patients had a one-year OS of 96% (95% CI, 90-100%) versus 63% (95% CI, 32-100%) for ctDNA-positive patients (Figure 3C).

Similarly, one-year progression-free survival (PFS) was 100% (95% CI, 100-100%) for pre-treatment ctDNA-negative patients and 85% (95% CI, 76-96%) for ctDNA-positive patients (Figure 3D). During-treatment ctDNA-negative patients had a one-year PFS of 100% (95% CI, 100-100%), compared to 78% (95% CI, 62-98%) for ctDNA-positive patients (Figure 3E). End-of-treatment ctDNA-negative patients had a one-year PFS of 92% (95% CI, 84-100%) versus 44% (95% CI, 17-100%) for ctDNA-positive patients (Figure 3F).

Locoregional failure (LRF) at one year was 0% (95% CI, undefined) among ctDNA-negative patients versus 11% (95% CI, 4-23%) among ctDNA-positive patients at pre-treatment (Figure 3G). Pre-treatment quantitative ctDNA was not associated with LRF (HR 1.0, 95% CI 0.99-1.00). At during-treatment, one-year LRF was 0% (95% CI, undefined) versus 19% (95% CI, 5-38%) for ctDNA-negative and ctDNA-positive groups, respectively (Figure 3H). At end-of-treatment, the one-year LRF was 6% (95% CI, 2-16%) for ctDNA-negative versus 39% (95% CI, 2-79%) in ctDNA-positive patients (Figure 3I).

When stratified by the timing of initial ctDNA clearance, patients who were ctDNA-negative at pre-treatment or who cleared ctDNA during-treatment had a one-year OS of 100% (95% CI, 100–100%; Figure 4A), one-year PFS of 100% (95% CI, 100–100%; Figure 4B), and one-year LRF rate of 0% (95% CI, undefined; Figure 4C). Among patients who cleared ctDNA only at end-of-treatment, one-year OS was 89% (95% CI, 75–100% Figure 4A), PFS was 81% (95% CI, 65–100%; Figure 4B), and LRF was 15% (95% CI, 4–35%; Figure 4C). Patients who were ctDNA-positive at end-of-treatment had significantly worse outcomes with one-year OS of 63% (95% CI, 32–100%), PFS of 44% (95% CI, 17–100%), and LRF of 39% (95% CI, 2–79%) (log-rank P=0.01 for OS and P=2.4x10-6 for PFS; Gray’s P=0.001 for LRF). All patients who were ctDNA-negative at end-of-treatment achieved a clinical complete response.

ctDNA Surveillance Monitoring
Seven patients developed molecular recurrence during the surveillance period after initially achieving clearance (Figure 5). All these patients subsequently experienced confirmed relapse, five locoregional and two distant, with ctDNA re-positivity consistently preceding radiographic or clinical evidence of recurrence by a median of 2.4 months (range 1-8.7 months). Because ctDNA re-positivity triggered off-schedule ‘enhanced’ assessments, the 2.4-month median lead time in the surveillance subset likely underestimates the biological lead time relative to standard NCCN. Among all patients who were persistently ctDNA-negative during the surveillance period, no treatment failure events occurred.
paper_content.methods:
Study Design and Participants
The institutional review and privacy boards of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK; IRB 16-370) and the University of South Florida (USF; IRB 004774) approved this cohort study with a waiver of informed consent. Patient confidentiality was maintained as required by the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA). Beginning in March 2021, adult patients (≥18 years) with biopsy-confirmed, non-metastatic ASCC were prospectively offered longitudinal ctDNA monitoring and all patients who provided informed consent to ctDNA testing were included. All patients were staged per the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC), 8th edition30 and received curative-intent CRT. Data collection concluded on July 31, 2024. Data sharing was governed by a three-way agreement among MSK, USF, and Natera, Inc., to allow data to be shared freely across all participating institutions, with the final dataset maintained at MSK.

Personalized mPCR-NGS ctDNA assay
A clinically validated, personalized, tumor-informed 16-plex mPCR-NGS assay (SignateraTM, Natera, Inc.) was used for the detection and quantification of ctDNA in blood samples.31 Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tumor tissue from surgical resection or biopsy samples and matched normal DNA extracted from a peripheral blood sample were processed for whole-exome sequencing to identify and track up to 16 patient-specific and tumor-specific somatic single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) in the associated patient’s plasma using a multiplex PCR-NGS approach. Cell-free DNA was extracted from patient plasma (median, 9.4 ml; range, 2.9–10.2 ml) at a given time point and was used to detect ctDNA. A plasma sample was classified as ctDNA-positive if two or more tumor-specific variants out of the 16 were detected above a predefined threshold. The predefined threshold is based on Natera’s proprietary variant calling method, wherein detecting at least two out of 16 variants ensures optimal analytical performance of the assay, with greater than 95% sensitivity at a mean variant allele frequency of 0.01% and 99.7% specificity.32 ctDNA concentration was reported as mean tumor molecules per milliliter (MTM/mL) of plasma. Testing cadence was at the discretion of the treating physician, with results available in real time. Lead time was defined as the interval between the first ctDNA re-positivity after a documented negative result and the date of first clinical or radiographic evidence of recurrence.

Treatment and Response Assessment
All patients received curative-intent CRT, typically with DP-IMRT. Radiation dose was adapted to tumor size: <2 cm, 50 Gy; 2–4 cm, 54 Gy; >4 cm, 58 Gy, all delivered in 2-Gy fractions.6 Most patients received concurrent fluoropyrimidine-based chemotherapy, with or without mitomycin, unless clinically contraindicated.

Treatment response was assessed 12–16 weeks after CRT using physical examination (including digital rectal and inguinal lymph node exams), anoproctoscopy, and cross-sectional imaging (MRI, CT, or PET-CT). Clinical complete response (cCR) was defined as no detectable tumor locally, regionally, or distantly. For patients with an incomplete but improving primary tumor response, short-interval re-evaluation (within 4–8 weeks) was permitted. Recurrence was defined as local, regional, or distant disease. Locoregional failure was defined as recurrence at the primary site or in pelvic/inguinal regional nodes, with ‘combined local–nodal failure’ reserved for concurrent recurrence at both sites. Salvage management for locoregional recurrence was categorized as operative salvage (APR), nonoperative salvage (re-irradiation and/or systemic therapy), or best supportive care for patients medically ineligible for salvage therapy.

Phlebotomy Timeline
Peripheral blood was collected at physician-defined intervals throughout the treatment course (Supplementary Figure 3). Pre-treatment samples were obtained at any point before treatment initiation or within five days after starting CRT. During-treatment samples were collected more than five days after CRT initiation but at least seven days before its completion. End-of-treatment samples were drawn from seven days before through 42 days after the end-of-CRT. Samples collected more than 42 days after CRT completion were categorized as surveillance timepoints. Patients who re-converted from negative to positive ctDNA status during surveillance underwent ‘enhanced surveillance’, including directed clinical examination (digital rectal examination and, when appropriate, flexible sigmoidoscopy/anoscopy) and expedited cross-sectional imaging (MR pelvis, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, and/or PET-CT).

Study Endpoints
The primary endpoint was OS, defined as the time from ctDNA assessment to death from any cause or to last follow-up. Secondary endpoints included progression-free survival and the cumulative incidence of locoregional failure. PFS was defined as the time from ctDNA assessment to the first occurrence of local or regional failure, distant metastasis, or death. LRF was defined as persistent, progressive, or recurrent disease in the primary tumor or regional lymph nodes, with death and distant recurrence treated as competing-risks.

Statistical Analyses
Baseline characteristics were summarized using medians and interquartile ranges (IQR) for continuous variables, and frequencies with percentages for categorical variables. Univariate logistic regression was used to evaluate predictors of pre-treatment ctDNA positivity. Kaplan-Meier estimates were used to evaluate OS and PFS from the date of end-of-treatment ctDNA assessment, stratifying patients by time of clearance. Additional timepoint-specific Kaplan-Meier analyses were conducted for OS and PFS according to ctDNA status at each sampling point, measured from the corresponding ctDNA collection date. Survival differences were compared using log-rank tests. LRF was analyzed at the same timepoints using competing-risk regression, with cumulative incidence curves by Gray’s test.

Patients without a ctDNA result at a given time point were excluded from time point-specific survival analyses. If multiple samples existed in a given phase (e.g., during-treatment), the most recent test was selected. In surveillance, if all ctDNA results were negative, the most recent was used; if any were ctDNA-positive, the first positive test was selected. Analyses were performed in R (v4.4.0) using tidyverse (v2.0.0), gtsummary (v2.0.0), ggsurvfit (v1.1.0), ggalluvial (v0.12.5), and ggpubr (v0.6.0).

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
To the authors,
The investigators have created a two-institution evaluation of 84 locally advanced anal CA patients and have obtained a
baseline tumor informed ctDNA and a post treatment post ctDNA and compared outcomes.
The authors concluded that a positive tumor informed ctDNA post treatment was associated with outcomes and should be
considered as part of the standard evaluation for response. The primary endpoint was OS; secondary endpoints were PFS
and LRF.
Comments:
• Please revise the statement: “….determining treatment response often requires up to six months of clinical and
radiographic follow-up.” I would suggest a revision of the verbiage “up to 6M may be required for serial evaluations to
determine optimal outcomes for sphincter preservation.”
• Was there a correlation of pretreatment ctDNA with AJCC staging?
• Of the 12 patients with recurrence, did they exhibit high-risk features? Tumor > 4 cm and/or lymph node positivity? Were
they compliant with their radiation? Did they have any dose reductions or delays?
• Was there any difference in outcomes for patients that were HPV negative?
• Was there any difference for the 7% of pts that did not receive MMC?
• I would recommend removing the one patient with the treatment that is unknown
• I think there is a mistake in your table re: HPV. It states 100% were positive or negative but 29 are unknown?
• 5-Fluorouracil is misspelled in the table C.
• Is the evaluation mid-treatment ctDNA necessary?
• The author states the use of ctDNA will allow “earlier escalation for high-risk patients, and de-intensification for molecular
responders”…. Are you suggesting that we should revise our surveillance or consider an APR sooner? I am not sure that a
positive ctDNA would convince patients to have their APR sooner if there is no evidence clinically for residual disease?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Reviewer Comments to the Authors
This manuscript addresses an important and practical topic in anal squamous cell carcinoma (ASCC) management,
evaluating a tumor informed circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) assay in a real world cohort. This study is a valuable
contribution, presenting real world data on tumor informed ctDNA testing in ASCC. Its strengths include prospective data
collection, excellent assay performance, and clinical relevance. To strengthen scientific rigor and interpretability, revisions
should address assay quantification, sampling timing, subgroup analyses, contextual comparison with HPV based assays,
and careful framing of conclusions.
Comments
1. Define the Negative Baseline Group and High Burden Misses
Please provide the characteristics of the ctDNA negative patients at baseline—particularly the 11% with high burden/stage
III disease. Were these predominantly HPV negative or did they have lower mutational burden? Can the authors clarify the
molecular and clinical details of this subgroup (e.g., mutation profiles, HPV status, stage distribution).
2. Assay Description and Quantitative Values
The manuscript currently provides only binary ctDNA status. Please include:
o The commercial name of the assay (e.g., Signatera™, Natera Inc.) in the Abstract and Methods.
o The reason for calling ctDNA positive (e.g., number of SNV targets).
o Include quantitative values such as median levels at baseline and during therapy in the text (only in Fig 2E currently), and
whether higher or lower ctDNA quantity, or rate of decline, correlates with outcomes. If there is a correlation with pre-
treatment level and outcome, it could be included in the multivariate analysis.
3. Timing of Sampling: Refinements Suggested
The definitions of baseline, mid treatment, and post treatment sampling are broad and could introduce bias.
o The time windows chosen allow for pre-treatment to occur 5 days after starting CRT, while post-treatment can be 7 days
before completion. The definitions used raise the question whether the dates were chosen post-hoc to influence the results.
Do the results change with the more commonly accepted definitions of pre and post treatment? I would suggest changing the
definition. Otherwise, consider renaming “mid-treatment” to “during treatment” and “post treatment” to “end of treatment” for
clarity.
o Specify how many patients had samples taken in the final week of treatment versus genuinely post treatment.
4. Sample Counts by Time Point
Please provide a clear breakdown of the number of patients with ctDNA results at each time point (baseline, during-
treatment, end-of-treatment, surveillance), including missing data and how these were handled in survival analyses.
5. Interpretation of Clearance and Clinical Applicability
While early ctDNA clearance is promising, caution is needed given the modest cohort size (84 patients), low event count (12
failures), and limited follow up (~18 months). Statements like “lays the foundation for integration into care” should be
tempered to reflect a hypothesis-generating study awaiting prospective validation.
6. Comparison with HPV ctDNA Assays
Please include a discussion comparing tumor informed ctDNA with HPV based ctDNA testing. For example, the TTMV HPV
DNA assay (Kabarriti et al., Cancers, 2025) demonstrated per patient surveillance sensitivity of 82.8%, specificity of 98.4%,
PPV of 96.0%, and NPV of 92.5%, with valuable quantitative ranges and lead time data pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov+1. How
might your approach compare in terms of sensitivity, specificity, and quantification, including in HPV-negative disease? It
would be ideal to provide outcomes for the HPV negative patients (approximately n=6). How did the assay perform at
baseline and during surveillance in this subgroup? This is important to distinguish your tumor informed approach from viral
targeted tests like NavRx.
7. ctDNA Detection of Recurrence During Surveillance
Confirm whether ctDNA positivity preceded all recurrences, including those detected during routine surveillance. Were there
any relapses not captured by ctDNA testing? If so, why might that have occurred? In the small cohort of patients with
negative pre-treatment ctDNA, was the surveillance testing useful?
8. False Negatives After Clearance
Patients who cleared ctDNA during treatment but later recurred suggest potential low disease burden below detection
threshold. Please discuss this limitation and whether alternative threshold levels (e.g., MTM/mL at a given time point) might
enhance prediction of durable remission. This area is a potential area of harm for clinicians, in that there may be a false
sense of assurance for a favorable outcome with a mid-treatment clearance, that could result in inappropriate treatment de-
escalation.
9. Testing Cadence and Clinical Influence
Since testing frequency was at physician discretion, clarify how this may have impacted results. Did ctDNA results ever
influence clinical decision making during the study? If so, please describe.
10. Avoid Overinterpretation
Rephrase any language suggesting that the assay is ready for routine clinical integration. Emphasize that findings support
the design of prospective trials rather than immediate practice changes.
11. Conflict of Interest and Industry Roles
Acknowledge in the relevant sections that six co authors are employees of Natera and clarify the company's role in assay
development, data collection, statistical analysis, and manuscript drafting.
12. Interpretation of cfDNA Plot
Please add a brief explanation for the cfDNA concentration plot (e.g., in Figure 2a). Specifically, note that although cfDNA
levels rise during treatment, ctDNA detection remains specific—highlighting assay robustness.

## Abstract

Patients with anal squamous cell carcinoma (ASCC) who fail chemoradiation (CRT) have poor outcomes, underscoring the need for biomarkers to guide risk stratification. In a real-world two-center cohort of 84 adults with non-metastatic ASCC treated with curative-intent CRT, we prospectively evaluate a tumor-informed circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) assay (SignateraTM, Natera). Here we show that across 647 plasma specimens, ctDNA is positive at pre-treatment in 79% (61/77), including 89% (24/27) with stage III disease. End-of-treatment ctDNA positivity identifies patients with inferior one-year outcomes: 63% overall survival, 44% progression-free survival, and 39% locoregional failure. Conversely, patients who were ctDNA-negative at baseline or who cleared ctDNA during-treatment have 100% locoregional failure-free survival. During surveillance, ctDNA re-emergence precedes clinical or radiographic relapse in every case. These findings support the consideration of ctDNA as a dynamic, treatment-responsive biomarker warranting prospective validation for risk-adapted surveillance and adjuvant therapy in ASCC.

---

## Introduction

Anal squamous cell carcinoma (ASCC) is a human papillomavirus (HPV)–associated malignancy for which definitive-intent (chemo)radiation (CRT) remains the standard treatment for non-metastatic disease.1-3 Although CRT often achieves long-term control and sphincter preservation, up to six months of serial evaluations may be required to assess treatment response.4 This prolonged interval may delay the detection of treatment failure, limit the window for effective salvage therapy, and contribute to patient anxiety and uncertainty in management. For patients with persistent or recurrent locoregional disease, salvage abdominoperineal resection (APR) remains the primary treatment, but it is associated with poor disease-specific and recurrence-free survival.5,6 These limitations underscore the need for early, reliable biomarkers to identify high-risk patients during or shortly after CRT, when timely therapeutic intervention may still improve outcomes.

Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) has emerged as a promising, minimally invasive blood-based biomarker that enables dynamic monitoring of disease burden through the detection of tumor-specific mutations in plasma.7-11 Prior studies in ASCC have predominantly focused on HPV-directed ctDNA assays,12-20 but these approaches may lack sensitivity in patients with HPV-negative (~5-10% of patients with ASCC).21,22 Tumor-informed ctDNA assays, customized to each patient’s unique mutational profile, may offer a more sensitive and broadly applicable alternative, although their utility in ASCC has not been well established yet.23,24

In this multicenter, real-world cohort study, we evaluated a commercially available, personalized, tumor-informed ctDNA assay for its prognostic and surveillance utility in patients with ASCC undergoing definitive-intent CRT. We hypothesized that ctDNA kinetics at pre-treatment, during-treatment, and end-of-treatment would correlate with clinical outcomes and, if validated, could inform risk-adapted, personalized treatment strategies.

---

## Results

Patient, Tumor, and Treatment Characteristics
Of 88 consecutive patients with localized ASCC who underwent definitive-intent dose-painted intensity-modulated radiation therapy (DP-IMRT), 84 patients (95%) had sufficient tumor tissue from diagnostic biopsies for ctDNA testing and were included in the final cohort (Figure 1A). Whole-exome sequencing (WES) identified key mutations across this population (Figure 1B). Demographic and treatment characteristics are summarized in Table 1 and Supplementary Table 1. The median follow-up among survivors, measured from diagnosis, was 18 months (interquartile range [IQR], 11–26 months).

ctDNA Detection and Temporal Dynamics
Across all timepoints, 647 plasma specimens were analyzed for ctDNA testing using a personalized, tumor-informed multiplex polymerase chain reaction-next-generation sequencing (mPCR-NGS) assay (SignateraTM) (Figure 1C). Cell-free DNA (cfDNA) concentrations increased during CRT, but ctDNA detection remained unaffected (Figure 1D). At pre-treatment, 79% (61 of 77) of patients were ctDNA-positive, including 89% (24 of 27) with stage III disease. Pre-treatment ctDNA positivity was significantly associated with T3/T4 tumors (odds ratio [OR], 4.08; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.01–27.6; P=0.049) and node-positive disease (OR, 8.33; 95% CI, 2.19–41.5; P=0.001) (Supplementary Table 2). As treatment progressed, ctDNA levels generally declined, though levels remained higher at each timepoint among patients with more advanced clinical stage, compared to stage I (Supplementary Figure 1 and Supplementary Table 3). Median ctDNA levels at pre-treatment, mid-treatment, and end-of-treatment were 1.02 MTM/mL (interquartile range (IQR), 0.17-25.43), 0 MTM/mL (IQR, 0-0.46), and 0 MTM/mL (IQR, 0-0). Of the end-of-treatment samples, 6 were drawn in the final week of CRT (−7 to -1 days), 7 on the final day of CRT (0 day), and 60 after CRT completion (+1 to +42 days) (Figure 1C).

Treatment Failure Events
The clinical courses of the cohort, grouped by baseline stage and outcome, are shown in Figure 2. Twelve patients (14%) experienced treatment failure (including death without progression) including seven locoregional failures, four distant failures, and one death (Supplementary Figure 2). Of the seven patients with locoregional failure, three had local-only failure, two had nodal-only failure, and two had combined local-nodal failure. Among patients with locoregional recurrence, three underwent salvage APR, two received nonoperative salvage with re-irradiation, and two were deemed medically ineligible for salvage therapy and was managed with best supportive care. Five deaths occurred in the post-CRT follow-up period. Four were attributed to disease progression including three from distant metastatic disease and one from locoregional recurrence as the patient died from complications of the recurrent tumor. At the last available disease assessment prior to death, all four had positive ctDNA. One additional patient died without evidence of disease progression due to complications of COVID-19 and Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile) colitis.

Among the 12 patients with treatment failure or death, 11 (92%) had at least one high-risk feature (tumor >4 cm and/or nodal involvement). All patients completed their prescribed course of CRT without dose reductions or treatment breaks. In a competing-risks analysis, absence of mitomycin at CRT and HPV status were not associated with increased hazard of locoregional recurrence (Supplementary Table 4). In all cases, ctDNA positivity preceded clinical or radiographic evidence of recurrence (Supplementary Figure 2). Notably, all patients who were ctDNA-negative at baseline remained recurrence-free during follow-up, suggesting this subgroup may represent particularly favorable biology.

Overall Survival, Progression-Free Survival, and Locoregional Failure
Pre-treatment ctDNA-negative patients had an estimated one-year overall survival (OS) of 100% (95% CI, 100-100%), compared to 97% (95% CI, 92-100%) for those with ctDNA-positive status (Figure 3A). Stratified by during-treatment ctDNA status, one-year OS was 100% (95% CI, 100-100%) for ctDNA-negative versus 93% (95 % CI, 84-100%) for ctDNA-positive patients (Figure 3B). At end-of-treatment, ctDNA-negative patients had a one-year OS of 96% (95% CI, 90-100%) versus 63% (95% CI, 32-100%) for ctDNA-positive patients (Figure 3C).

Similarly, one-year progression-free survival (PFS) was 100% (95% CI, 100-100%) for pre-treatment ctDNA-negative patients and 85% (95% CI, 76-96%) for ctDNA-positive patients (Figure 3D). During-treatment ctDNA-negative patients had a one-year PFS of 100% (95% CI, 100-100%), compared to 78% (95% CI, 62-98%) for ctDNA-positive patients (Figure 3E). End-of-treatment ctDNA-negative patients had a one-year PFS of 92% (95% CI, 84-100%) versus 44% (95% CI, 17-100%) for ctDNA-positive patients (Figure 3F).

Locoregional failure (LRF) at one year was 0% (95% CI, undefined) among ctDNA-negative patients versus 11% (95% CI, 4-23%) among ctDNA-positive patients at pre-treatment (Figure 3G). Pre-treatment quantitative ctDNA was not associated with LRF (HR 1.0, 95% CI 0.99-1.00). At during-treatment, one-year LRF was 0% (95% CI, undefined) versus 19% (95% CI, 5-38%) for ctDNA-negative and ctDNA-positive groups, respectively (Figure 3H). At end-of-treatment, the one-year LRF was 6% (95% CI, 2-16%) for ctDNA-negative versus 39% (95% CI, 2-79%) in ctDNA-positive patients (Figure 3I).

When stratified by the timing of initial ctDNA clearance, patients who were ctDNA-negative at pre-treatment or who cleared ctDNA during-treatment had a one-year OS of 100% (95% CI, 100–100%; Figure 4A), one-year PFS of 100% (95% CI, 100–100%; Figure 4B), and one-year LRF rate of 0% (95% CI, undefined; Figure 4C). Among patients who cleared ctDNA only at end-of-treatment, one-year OS was 89% (95% CI, 75–100% Figure 4A), PFS was 81% (95% CI, 65–100%; Figure 4B), and LRF was 15% (95% CI, 4–35%; Figure 4C). Patients who were ctDNA-positive at end-of-treatment had significantly worse outcomes with one-year OS of 63% (95% CI, 32–100%), PFS of 44% (95% CI, 17–100%), and LRF of 39% (95% CI, 2–79%) (log-rank P=0.01 for OS and P=2.4x10-6 for PFS; Gray’s P=0.001 for LRF). All patients who were ctDNA-negative at end-of-treatment achieved a clinical complete response.

ctDNA Surveillance Monitoring
Seven patients developed molecular recurrence during the surveillance period after initially achieving clearance (Figure 5). All these patients subsequently experienced confirmed relapse, five locoregional and two distant, with ctDNA re-positivity consistently preceding radiographic or clinical evidence of recurrence by a median of 2.4 months (range 1-8.7 months). Because ctDNA re-positivity triggered off-schedule ‘enhanced’ assessments, the 2.4-month median lead time in the surveillance subset likely underestimates the biological lead time relative to standard NCCN. Among all patients who were persistently ctDNA-negative during the surveillance period, no treatment failure events occurred.

---

## Methods

Study Design and Participants
The institutional review and privacy boards of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK; IRB 16-370) and the University of South Florida (USF; IRB 004774) approved this cohort study with a waiver of informed consent. Patient confidentiality was maintained as required by the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA). Beginning in March 2021, adult patients (≥18 years) with biopsy-confirmed, non-metastatic ASCC were prospectively offered longitudinal ctDNA monitoring and all patients who provided informed consent to ctDNA testing were included. All patients were staged per the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC), 8th edition30 and received curative-intent CRT. Data collection concluded on July 31, 2024. Data sharing was governed by a three-way agreement among MSK, USF, and Natera, Inc., to allow data to be shared freely across all participating institutions, with the final dataset maintained at MSK.

Personalized mPCR-NGS ctDNA assay
A clinically validated, personalized, tumor-informed 16-plex mPCR-NGS assay (SignateraTM, Natera, Inc.) was used for the detection and quantification of ctDNA in blood samples.31 Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tumor tissue from surgical resection or biopsy samples and matched normal DNA extracted from a peripheral blood sample were processed for whole-exome sequencing to identify and track up to 16 patient-specific and tumor-specific somatic single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) in the associated patient’s plasma using a multiplex PCR-NGS approach. Cell-free DNA was extracted from patient plasma (median, 9.4 ml; range, 2.9–10.2 ml) at a given time point and was used to detect ctDNA. A plasma sample was classified as ctDNA-positive if two or more tumor-specific variants out of the 16 were detected above a predefined threshold. The predefined threshold is based on Natera’s proprietary variant calling method, wherein detecting at least two out of 16 variants ensures optimal analytical performance of the assay, with greater than 95% sensitivity at a mean variant allele frequency of 0.01% and 99.7% specificity.32 ctDNA concentration was reported as mean tumor molecules per milliliter (MTM/mL) of plasma. Testing cadence was at the discretion of the treating physician, with results available in real time. Lead time was defined as the interval between the first ctDNA re-positivity after a documented negative result and the date of first clinical or radiographic evidence of recurrence.

Treatment and Response Assessment
All patients received curative-intent CRT, typically with DP-IMRT. Radiation dose was adapted to tumor size: <2 cm, 50 Gy; 2–4 cm, 54 Gy; >4 cm, 58 Gy, all delivered in 2-Gy fractions.6 Most patients received concurrent fluoropyrimidine-based chemotherapy, with or without mitomycin, unless clinically contraindicated.

Treatment response was assessed 12–16 weeks after CRT using physical examination (including digital rectal and inguinal lymph node exams), anoproctoscopy, and cross-sectional imaging (MRI, CT, or PET-CT). Clinical complete response (cCR) was defined as no detectable tumor locally, regionally, or distantly. For patients with an incomplete but improving primary tumor response, short-interval re-evaluation (within 4–8 weeks) was permitted. Recurrence was defined as local, regional, or distant disease. Locoregional failure was defined as recurrence at the primary site or in pelvic/inguinal regional nodes, with ‘combined local–nodal failure’ reserved for concurrent recurrence at both sites. Salvage management for locoregional recurrence was categorized as operative salvage (APR), nonoperative salvage (re-irradiation and/or systemic therapy), or best supportive care for patients medically ineligible for salvage therapy.

Phlebotomy Timeline
Peripheral blood was collected at physician-defined intervals throughout the treatment course (Supplementary Figure 3). Pre-treatment samples were obtained at any point before treatment initiation or within five days after starting CRT. During-treatment samples were collected more than five days after CRT initiation but at least seven days before its completion. End-of-treatment samples were drawn from seven days before through 42 days after the end-of-CRT. Samples collected more than 42 days after CRT completion were categorized as surveillance timepoints. Patients who re-converted from negative to positive ctDNA status during surveillance underwent ‘enhanced surveillance’, including directed clinical examination (digital rectal examination and, when appropriate, flexible sigmoidoscopy/anoscopy) and expedited cross-sectional imaging (MR pelvis, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, and/or PET-CT).

Study Endpoints
The primary endpoint was OS, defined as the time from ctDNA assessment to death from any cause or to last follow-up. Secondary endpoints included progression-free survival and the cumulative incidence of locoregional failure. PFS was defined as the time from ctDNA assessment to the first occurrence of local or regional failure, distant metastasis, or death. LRF was defined as persistent, progressive, or recurrent disease in the primary tumor or regional lymph nodes, with death and distant recurrence treated as competing-risks.

Statistical Analyses
Baseline characteristics were summarized using medians and interquartile ranges (IQR) for continuous variables, and frequencies with percentages for categorical variables. Univariate logistic regression was used to evaluate predictors of pre-treatment ctDNA positivity. Kaplan-Meier estimates were used to evaluate OS and PFS from the date of end-of-treatment ctDNA assessment, stratifying patients by time of clearance. Additional timepoint-specific Kaplan-Meier analyses were conducted for OS and PFS according to ctDNA status at each sampling point, measured from the corresponding ctDNA collection date. Survival differences were compared using log-rank tests. LRF was analyzed at the same timepoints using competing-risk regression, with cumulative incidence curves by Gray’s test.

Patients without a ctDNA result at a given time point were excluded from time point-specific survival analyses. If multiple samples existed in a given phase (e.g., during-treatment), the most recent test was selected. In surveillance, if all ctDNA results were negative, the most recent was used; if any were ctDNA-positive, the first positive test was selected. Analyses were performed in R (v4.4.0) using tidyverse (v2.0.0), gtsummary (v2.0.0), ggsurvfit (v1.1.0), ggalluvial (v0.12.5), and ggpubr (v0.6.0).

## Paper

## Abstract

Patients with anal squamous cell carcinoma (ASCC) who fail chemoradiation (CRT) have poor outcomes, underscoring the need for biomarkers to guide risk stratification. In a real-world two-center cohort of 84 adults with non-metastatic ASCC treated with curative-intent CRT, we prospectively evaluate a tumor-informed circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) assay (SignateraTM, Natera). Here we show that across 647 plasma specimens, ctDNA is positive at pre-treatment in 79% (61/77), including 89% (24/27) with stage III disease. End-of-treatment ctDNA positivity identifies patients with inferior one-year outcomes: 63% overall survival, 44% progression-free survival, and 39% locoregional failure. Conversely, patients who were ctDNA-negative at baseline or who cleared ctDNA during-treatment have 100% locoregional failure-free survival. During surveillance, ctDNA re-emergence precedes clinical or radiographic relapse in every case. These findings support the consideration of ctDNA as a dynamic, treatment-responsive biomarker warranting prospective validation for risk-adapted surveillance and adjuvant therapy in ASCC.

---

## Introduction

Anal squamous cell carcinoma (ASCC) is a human papillomavirus (HPV)–associated malignancy for which definitive-intent (chemo)radiation (CRT) remains the standard treatment for non-metastatic disease.1-3 Although CRT often achieves long-term control and sphincter preservation, up to six months of serial evaluations may be required to assess treatment response.4 This prolonged interval may delay the detection of treatment failure, limit the window for effective salvage therapy, and contribute to patient anxiety and uncertainty in management. For patients with persistent or recurrent locoregional disease, salvage abdominoperineal resection (APR) remains the primary treatment, but it is associated with poor disease-specific and recurrence-free survival.5,6 These limitations underscore the need for early, reliable biomarkers to identify high-risk patients during or shortly after CRT, when timely therapeutic intervention may still improve outcomes.

Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) has emerged as a promising, minimally invasive blood-based biomarker that enables dynamic monitoring of disease burden through the detection of tumor-specific mutations in plasma.7-11 Prior studies in ASCC have predominantly focused on HPV-directed ctDNA assays,12-20 but these approaches may lack sensitivity in patients with HPV-negative (~5-10% of patients with ASCC).21,22 Tumor-informed ctDNA assays, customized to each patient’s unique mutational profile, may offer a more sensitive and broadly applicable alternative, although their utility in ASCC has not been well established yet.23,24

In this multicenter, real-world cohort study, we evaluated a commercially available, personalized, tumor-informed ctDNA assay for its prognostic and surveillance utility in patients with ASCC undergoing definitive-intent CRT. We hypothesized that ctDNA kinetics at pre-treatment, during-treatment, and end-of-treatment would correlate with clinical outcomes and, if validated, could inform risk-adapted, personalized treatment strategies.

---

## Results

Patient, Tumor, and Treatment Characteristics
Of 88 consecutive patients with localized ASCC who underwent definitive-intent dose-painted intensity-modulated radiation therapy (DP-IMRT), 84 patients (95%) had sufficient tumor tissue from diagnostic biopsies for ctDNA testing and were included in the final cohort (Figure 1A). Whole-exome sequencing (WES) identified key mutations across this population (Figure 1B). Demographic and treatment characteristics are summarized in Table 1 and Supplementary Table 1. The median follow-up among survivors, measured from diagnosis, was 18 months (interquartile range [IQR], 11–26 months).

ctDNA Detection and Temporal Dynamics
Across all timepoints, 647 plasma specimens were analyzed for ctDNA testing using a personalized, tumor-informed multiplex polymerase chain reaction-next-generation sequencing (mPCR-NGS) assay (SignateraTM) (Figure 1C). Cell-free DNA (cfDNA) concentrations increased during CRT, but ctDNA detection remained unaffected (Figure 1D). At pre-treatment, 79% (61 of 77) of patients were ctDNA-positive, including 89% (24 of 27) with stage III disease. Pre-treatment ctDNA positivity was significantly associated with T3/T4 tumors (odds ratio [OR], 4.08; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.01–27.6; P=0.049) and node-positive disease (OR, 8.33; 95% CI, 2.19–41.5; P=0.001) (Supplementary Table 2). As treatment progressed, ctDNA levels generally declined, though levels remained higher at each timepoint among patients with more advanced clinical stage, compared to stage I (Supplementary Figure 1 and Supplementary Table 3). Median ctDNA levels at pre-treatment, mid-treatment, and end-of-treatment were 1.02 MTM/mL (interquartile range (IQR), 0.17-25.43), 0 MTM/mL (IQR, 0-0.46), and 0 MTM/mL (IQR, 0-0). Of the end-of-treatment samples, 6 were drawn in the final week of CRT (−7 to -1 days), 7 on the final day of CRT (0 day), and 60 after CRT completion (+1 to +42 days) (Figure 1C).

Treatment Failure Events
The clinical courses of the cohort, grouped by baseline stage and outcome, are shown in Figure 2. Twelve patients (14%) experienced treatment failure (including death without progression) including seven locoregional failures, four distant failures, and one death (Supplementary Figure 2). Of the seven patients with locoregional failure, three had local-only failure, two had nodal-only failure, and two had combined local-nodal failure. Among patients with locoregional recurrence, three underwent salvage APR, two received nonoperative salvage with re-irradiation, and two were deemed medically ineligible for salvage therapy and was managed with best supportive care. Five deaths occurred in the post-CRT follow-up period. Four were attributed to disease progression including three from distant metastatic disease and one from locoregional recurrence as the patient died from complications of the recurrent tumor. At the last available disease assessment prior to death, all four had positive ctDNA. One additional patient died without evidence of disease progression due to complications of COVID-19 and Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile) colitis.

Among the 12 patients with treatment failure or death, 11 (92%) had at least one high-risk feature (tumor >4 cm and/or nodal involvement). All patients completed their prescribed course of CRT without dose reductions or treatment breaks. In a competing-risks analysis, absence of mitomycin at CRT and HPV status were not associated with increased hazard of locoregional recurrence (Supplementary Table 4). In all cases, ctDNA positivity preceded clinical or radiographic evidence of recurrence (Supplementary Figure 2). Notably, all patients who were ctDNA-negative at baseline remained recurrence-free during follow-up, suggesting this subgroup may represent particularly favorable biology.

Overall Survival, Progression-Free Survival, and Locoregional Failure
Pre-treatment ctDNA-negative patients had an estimated one-year overall survival (OS) of 100% (95% CI, 100-100%), compared to 97% (95% CI, 92-100%) for those with ctDNA-positive status (Figure 3A). Stratified by during-treatment ctDNA status, one-year OS was 100% (95% CI, 100-100%) for ctDNA-negative versus 93% (95 % CI, 84-100%) for ctDNA-positive patients (Figure 3B). At end-of-treatment, ctDNA-negative patients had a one-year OS of 96% (95% CI, 90-100%) versus 63% (95% CI, 32-100%) for ctDNA-positive patients (Figure 3C).

Similarly, one-year progression-free survival (PFS) was 100% (95% CI, 100-100%) for pre-treatment ctDNA-negative patients and 85% (95% CI, 76-96%) for ctDNA-positive patients (Figure 3D). During-treatment ctDNA-negative patients had a one-year PFS of 100% (95% CI, 100-100%), compared to 78% (95% CI, 62-98%) for ctDNA-positive patients (Figure 3E). End-of-treatment ctDNA-negative patients had a one-year PFS of 92% (95% CI, 84-100%) versus 44% (95% CI, 17-100%) for ctDNA-positive patients (Figure 3F).

Locoregional failure (LRF) at one year was 0% (95% CI, undefined) among ctDNA-negative patients versus 11% (95% CI, 4-23%) among ctDNA-positive patients at pre-treatment (Figure 3G). Pre-treatment quantitative ctDNA was not associated with LRF (HR 1.0, 95% CI 0.99-1.00). At during-treatment, one-year LRF was 0% (95% CI, undefined) versus 19% (95% CI, 5-38%) for ctDNA-negative and ctDNA-positive groups, respectively (Figure 3H). At end-of-treatment, the one-year LRF was 6% (95% CI, 2-16%) for ctDNA-negative versus 39% (95% CI, 2-79%) in ctDNA-positive patients (Figure 3I).

When stratified by the timing of initial ctDNA clearance, patients who were ctDNA-negative at pre-treatment or who cleared ctDNA during-treatment had a one-year OS of 100% (95% CI, 100–100%; Figure 4A), one-year PFS of 100% (95% CI, 100–100%; Figure 4B), and one-year LRF rate of 0% (95% CI, undefined; Figure 4C). Among patients who cleared ctDNA only at end-of-treatment, one-year OS was 89% (95% CI, 75–100% Figure 4A), PFS was 81% (95% CI, 65–100%; Figure 4B), and LRF was 15% (95% CI, 4–35%; Figure 4C). Patients who were ctDNA-positive at end-of-treatment had significantly worse outcomes with one-year OS of 63% (95% CI, 32–100%), PFS of 44% (95% CI, 17–100%), and LRF of 39% (95% CI, 2–79%) (log-rank P=0.01 for OS and P=2.4x10-6 for PFS; Gray’s P=0.001 for LRF). All patients who were ctDNA-negative at end-of-treatment achieved a clinical complete response.

ctDNA Surveillance Monitoring
Seven patients developed molecular recurrence during the surveillance period after initially achieving clearance (Figure 5). All these patients subsequently experienced confirmed relapse, five locoregional and two distant, with ctDNA re-positivity consistently preceding radiographic or clinical evidence of recurrence by a median of 2.4 months (range 1-8.7 months). Because ctDNA re-positivity triggered off-schedule ‘enhanced’ assessments, the 2.4-month median lead time in the surveillance subset likely underestimates the biological lead time relative to standard NCCN. Among all patients who were persistently ctDNA-negative during the surveillance period, no treatment failure events occurred.

## Methods

Study Design and Participants
The institutional review and privacy boards of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK; IRB 16-370) and the University of South Florida (USF; IRB 004774) approved this cohort study with a waiver of informed consent. Patient confidentiality was maintained as required by the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA). Beginning in March 2021, adult patients (≥18 years) with biopsy-confirmed, non-metastatic ASCC were prospectively offered longitudinal ctDNA monitoring and all patients who provided informed consent to ctDNA testing were included. All patients were staged per the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC), 8th edition30 and received curative-intent CRT. Data collection concluded on July 31, 2024. Data sharing was governed by a three-way agreement among MSK, USF, and Natera, Inc., to allow data to be shared freely across all participating institutions, with the final dataset maintained at MSK.

Personalized mPCR-NGS ctDNA assay
A clinically validated, personalized, tumor-informed 16-plex mPCR-NGS assay (SignateraTM, Natera, Inc.) was used for the detection and quantification of ctDNA in blood samples.31 Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tumor tissue from surgical resection or biopsy samples and matched normal DNA extracted from a peripheral blood sample were processed for whole-exome sequencing to identify and track up to 16 patient-specific and tumor-specific somatic single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) in the associated patient’s plasma using a multiplex PCR-NGS approach. Cell-free DNA was extracted from patient plasma (median, 9.4 ml; range, 2.9–10.2 ml) at a given time point and was used to detect ctDNA. A plasma sample was classified as ctDNA-positive if two or more tumor-specific variants out of the 16 were detected above a predefined threshold. The predefined threshold is based on Natera’s proprietary variant calling method, wherein detecting at least two out of 16 variants ensures optimal analytical performance of the assay, with greater than 95% sensitivity at a mean variant allele frequency of 0.01% and 99.7% specificity.32 ctDNA concentration was reported as mean tumor molecules per milliliter (MTM/mL) of plasma. Testing cadence was at the discretion of the treating physician, with results available in real time. Lead time was defined as the interval between the first ctDNA re-positivity after a documented negative result and the date of first clinical or radiographic evidence of recurrence.

Treatment and Response Assessment
All patients received curative-intent CRT, typically with DP-IMRT. Radiation dose was adapted to tumor size: <2 cm, 50 Gy; 2–4 cm, 54 Gy; >4 cm, 58 Gy, all delivered in 2-Gy fractions.6 Most patients received concurrent fluoropyrimidine-based chemotherapy, with or without mitomycin, unless clinically contraindicated.

Treatment response was assessed 12–16 weeks after CRT using physical examination (including digital rectal and inguinal lymph node exams), anoproctoscopy, and cross-sectional imaging (MRI, CT, or PET-CT). Clinical complete response (cCR) was defined as no detectable tumor locally, regionally, or distantly. For patients with an incomplete but improving primary tumor response, short-interval re-evaluation (within 4–8 weeks) was permitted. Recurrence was defined as local, regional, or distant disease. Locoregional failure was defined as recurrence at the primary site or in pelvic/inguinal regional nodes, with ‘combined local–nodal failure’ reserved for concurrent recurrence at both sites. Salvage management for locoregional recurrence was categorized as operative salvage (APR), nonoperative salvage (re-irradiation and/or systemic therapy), or best supportive care for patients medically ineligible for salvage therapy.

Phlebotomy Timeline
Peripheral blood was collected at physician-defined intervals throughout the treatment course (Supplementary Figure 3). Pre-treatment samples were obtained at any point before treatment initiation or within five days after starting CRT. During-treatment samples were collected more than five days after CRT initiation but at least seven days before its completion. End-of-treatment samples were drawn from seven days before through 42 days after the end-of-CRT. Samples collected more than 42 days after CRT completion were categorized as surveillance timepoints. Patients who re-converted from negative to positive ctDNA status during surveillance underwent ‘enhanced surveillance’, including directed clinical examination (digital rectal examination and, when appropriate, flexible sigmoidoscopy/anoscopy) and expedited cross-sectional imaging (MR pelvis, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, and/or PET-CT).

Study Endpoints
The primary endpoint was OS, defined as the time from ctDNA assessment to death from any cause or to last follow-up. Secondary endpoints included progression-free survival and the cumulative incidence of locoregional failure. PFS was defined as the time from ctDNA assessment to the first occurrence of local or regional failure, distant metastasis, or death. LRF was defined as persistent, progressive, or recurrent disease in the primary tumor or regional lymph nodes, with death and distant recurrence treated as competing-risks.

Statistical Analyses
Baseline characteristics were summarized using medians and interquartile ranges (IQR) for continuous variables, and frequencies with percentages for categorical variables. Univariate logistic regression was used to evaluate predictors of pre-treatment ctDNA positivity. Kaplan-Meier estimates were used to evaluate OS and PFS from the date of end-of-treatment ctDNA assessment, stratifying patients by time of clearance. Additional timepoint-specific Kaplan-Meier analyses were conducted for OS and PFS according to ctDNA status at each sampling point, measured from the corresponding ctDNA collection date. Survival differences were compared using log-rank tests. LRF was analyzed at the same timepoints using competing-risk regression, with cumulative incidence curves by Gray’s test.

Patients without a ctDNA result at a given time point were excluded from time point-specific survival analyses. If multiple samples existed in a given phase (e.g., during-treatment), the most recent test was selected. In surveillance, if all ctDNA results were negative, the most recent was used; if any were ctDNA-positive, the first positive test was selected. Analyses were performed in R (v4.4.0) using tidyverse (v2.0.0), gtsummary (v2.0.0), ggsurvfit (v1.1.0), ggalluvial (v0.12.5), and ggpubr (v0.6.0).

## Paper

## Abstract

Patients with anal squamous cell carcinoma (ASCC) who fail chemoradiation (CRT) have poor outcomes, underscoring the need for biomarkers to guide risk stratification. In a real-world two-center cohort of 84 adults with non-metastatic ASCC treated with curative-intent CRT, we prospectively evaluate a tumor-informed circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) assay (SignateraTM, Natera). Here we show that across 647 plasma specimens, ctDNA is positive at pre-treatment in 79% (61/77), including 89% (24/27) with stage III disease. End-of-treatment ctDNA positivity identifies patients with inferior one-year outcomes: 63% overall survival, 44% progression-free survival, and 39% locoregional failure. Conversely, patients who were ctDNA-negative at baseline or who cleared ctDNA during-treatment have 100% locoregional failure-free survival. During surveillance, ctDNA re-emergence precedes clinical or radiographic relapse in every case. These findings support the consideration of ctDNA as a dynamic, treatment-responsive biomarker warranting prospective validation for risk-adapted surveillance and adjuvant therapy in ASCC.

---

## Introduction

Anal squamous cell carcinoma (ASCC) is a human papillomavirus (HPV)–associated malignancy for which definitive-intent (chemo)radiation (CRT) remains the standard treatment for non-metastatic disease.1-3 Although CRT often achieves long-term control and sphincter preservation, up to six months of serial evaluations may be required to assess treatment response.4 This prolonged interval may delay the detection of treatment failure, limit the window for effective salvage therapy, and contribute to patient anxiety and uncertainty in management. For patients with persistent or recurrent locoregional disease, salvage abdominoperineal resection (APR) remains the primary treatment, but it is associated with poor disease-specific and recurrence-free survival.5,6 These limitations underscore the need for early, reliable biomarkers to identify high-risk patients during or shortly after CRT, when timely therapeutic intervention may still improve outcomes.

Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) has emerged as a promising, minimally invasive blood-based biomarker that enables dynamic monitoring of disease burden through the detection of tumor-specific mutations in plasma.7-11 Prior studies in ASCC have predominantly focused on HPV-directed ctDNA assays,12-20 but these approaches may lack sensitivity in patients with HPV-negative (~5-10% of patients with ASCC).21,22 Tumor-informed ctDNA assays, customized to each patient’s unique mutational profile, may offer a more sensitive and broadly applicable alternative, although their utility in ASCC has not been well established yet.23,24

In this multicenter, real-world cohort study, we evaluated a commercially available, personalized, tumor-informed ctDNA assay for its prognostic and surveillance utility in patients with ASCC undergoing definitive-intent CRT. We hypothesized that ctDNA kinetics at pre-treatment, during-treatment, and end-of-treatment would correlate with clinical outcomes and, if validated, could inform risk-adapted, personalized treatment strategies.

---

## Results

Patient, Tumor, and Treatment Characteristics
Of 88 consecutive patients with localized ASCC who underwent definitive-intent dose-painted intensity-modulated radiation therapy (DP-IMRT), 84 patients (95%) had sufficient tumor tissue from diagnostic biopsies for ctDNA testing and were included in the final cohort (Figure 1A). Whole-exome sequencing (WES) identified key mutations across this population (Figure 1B). Demographic and treatment characteristics are summarized in Table 1 and Supplementary Table 1. The median follow-up among survivors, measured from diagnosis, was 18 months (interquartile range [IQR], 11–26 months).

ctDNA Detection and Temporal Dynamics
Across all timepoints, 647 plasma specimens were analyzed for ctDNA testing using a personalized, tumor-informed multiplex polymerase chain reaction-next-generation sequencing (mPCR-NGS) assay (SignateraTM) (Figure 1C). Cell-free DNA (cfDNA) concentrations increased during CRT, but ctDNA detection remained unaffected (Figure 1D). At pre-treatment, 79% (61 of 77) of patients were ctDNA-positive, including 89% (24 of 27) with stage III disease. Pre-treatment ctDNA positivity was significantly associated with T3/T4 tumors (odds ratio [OR], 4.08; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.01–27.6; P=0.049) and node-positive disease (OR, 8.33; 95% CI, 2.19–41.5; P=0.001) (Supplementary Table 2). As treatment progressed, ctDNA levels generally declined, though levels remained higher at each timepoint among patients with more advanced clinical stage, compared to stage I (Supplementary Figure 1 and Supplementary Table 3). Median ctDNA levels at pre-treatment, mid-treatment, and end-of-treatment were 1.02 MTM/mL (interquartile range (IQR), 0.17-25.43), 0 MTM/mL (IQR, 0-0.46), and 0 MTM/mL (IQR, 0-0). Of the end-of-treatment samples, 6 were drawn in the final week of CRT (−7 to -1 days), 7 on the final day of CRT (0 day), and 60 after CRT completion (+1 to +42 days) (Figure 1C).

Treatment Failure Events
The clinical courses of the cohort, grouped by baseline stage and outcome, are shown in Figure 2. Twelve patients (14%) experienced treatment failure (including death without progression) including seven locoregional failures, four distant failures, and one death (Supplementary Figure 2). Of the seven patients with locoregional failure, three had local-only failure, two had nodal-only failure, and two had combined local-nodal failure. Among patients with locoregional recurrence, three underwent salvage APR, two received nonoperative salvage with re-irradiation, and two were deemed medically ineligible for salvage therapy and was managed with best supportive care. Five deaths occurred in the post-CRT follow-up period. Four were attributed to disease progression including three from distant metastatic disease and one from locoregional recurrence as the patient died from complications of the recurrent tumor. At the last available disease assessment prior to death, all four had positive ctDNA. One additional patient died without evidence of disease progression due to complications of COVID-19 and Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile) colitis.

Among the 12 patients with treatment failure or death, 11 (92%) had at least one high-risk feature (tumor >4 cm and/or nodal involvement). All patients completed their prescribed course of CRT without dose reductions or treatment breaks. In a competing-risks analysis, absence of mitomycin at CRT and HPV status were not associated with increased hazard of locoregional recurrence (Supplementary Table 4). In all cases, ctDNA positivity preceded clinical or radiographic evidence of recurrence (Supplementary Figure 2). Notably, all patients who were ctDNA-negative at baseline remained recurrence-free during follow-up, suggesting this subgroup may represent particularly favorable biology.

Overall Survival, Progression-Free Survival, and Locoregional Failure
Pre-treatment ctDNA-negative patients had an estimated one-year overall survival (OS) of 100% (95% CI, 100-100%), compared to 97% (95% CI, 92-100%) for those with ctDNA-positive status (Figure 3A). Stratified by during-treatment ctDNA status, one-year OS was 100% (95% CI, 100-100%) for ctDNA-negative versus 93% (95 % CI, 84-100%) for ctDNA-positive patients (Figure 3B). At end-of-treatment, ctDNA-negative patients had a one-year OS of 96% (95% CI, 90-100%) versus 63% (95% CI, 32-100%) for ctDNA-positive patients (Figure 3C).

Similarly, one-year progression-free survival (PFS) was 100% (95% CI, 100-100%) for pre-treatment ctDNA-negative patients and 85% (95% CI, 76-96%) for ctDNA-positive patients (Figure 3D). During-treatment ctDNA-negative patients had a one-year PFS of 100% (95% CI, 100-100%), compared to 78% (95% CI, 62-98%) for ctDNA-positive patients (Figure 3E). End-of-treatment ctDNA-negative patients had a one-year PFS of 92% (95% CI, 84-100%) versus 44% (95% CI, 17-100%) for ctDNA-positive patients (Figure 3F).

Locoregional failure (LRF) at one year was 0% (95% CI, undefined) among ctDNA-negative patients versus 11% (95% CI, 4-23%) among ctDNA-positive patients at pre-treatment (Figure 3G). Pre-treatment quantitative ctDNA was not associated with LRF (HR 1.0, 95% CI 0.99-1.00). At during-treatment, one-year LRF was 0% (95% CI, undefined) versus 19% (95% CI, 5-38%) for ctDNA-negative and ctDNA-positive groups, respectively (Figure 3H). At end-of-treatment, the one-year LRF was 6% (95% CI, 2-16%) for ctDNA-negative versus 39% (95% CI, 2-79%) in ctDNA-positive patients (Figure 3I).

When stratified by the timing of initial ctDNA clearance, patients who were ctDNA-negative at pre-treatment or who cleared ctDNA during-treatment had a one-year OS of 100% (95% CI, 100–100%; Figure 4A), one-year PFS of 100% (95% CI, 100–100%; Figure 4B), and one-year LRF rate of 0% (95% CI, undefined; Figure 4C). Among patients who cleared ctDNA only at end-of-treatment, one-year OS was 89% (95% CI, 75–100% Figure 4A), PFS was 81% (95% CI, 65–100%; Figure 4B), and LRF was 15% (95% CI, 4–35%; Figure 4C). Patients who were ctDNA-positive at end-of-treatment had significantly worse outcomes with one-year OS of 63% (95% CI, 32–100%), PFS of 44% (95% CI, 17–100%), and LRF of 39% (95% CI, 2–79%) (log-rank P=0.01 for OS and P=2.4x10-6 for PFS; Gray’s P=0.001 for LRF). All patients who were ctDNA-negative at end-of-treatment achieved a clinical complete response.

ctDNA Surveillance Monitoring
Seven patients developed molecular recurrence during the surveillance period after initially achieving clearance (Figure 5). All these patients subsequently experienced confirmed relapse, five locoregional and two distant, with ctDNA re-positivity consistently preceding radiographic or clinical evidence of recurrence by a median of 2.4 months (range 1-8.7 months). Because ctDNA re-positivity triggered off-schedule ‘enhanced’ assessments, the 2.4-month median lead time in the surveillance subset likely underestimates the biological lead time relative to standard NCCN. Among all patients who were persistently ctDNA-negative during the surveillance period, no treatment failure events occurred.

---

## Methods

Study Design and Participants
The institutional review and privacy boards of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK; IRB 16-370) and the University of South Florida (USF; IRB 004774) approved this cohort study with a waiver of informed consent. Patient confidentiality was maintained as required by the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA). Beginning in March 2021, adult patients (≥18 years) with biopsy-confirmed, non-metastatic ASCC were prospectively offered longitudinal ctDNA monitoring and all patients who provided informed consent to ctDNA testing were included. All patients were staged per the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC), 8th edition30 and received curative-intent CRT. Data collection concluded on July 31, 2024. Data sharing was governed by a three-way agreement among MSK, USF, and Natera, Inc., to allow data to be shared freely across all participating institutions, with the final dataset maintained at MSK.

Personalized mPCR-NGS ctDNA assay
A clinically validated, personalized, tumor-informed 16-plex mPCR-NGS assay (SignateraTM, Natera, Inc.) was used for the detection and quantification of ctDNA in blood samples.31 Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tumor tissue from surgical resection or biopsy samples and matched normal DNA extracted from a peripheral blood sample were processed for whole-exome sequencing to identify and track up to 16 patient-specific and tumor-specific somatic single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) in the associated patient’s plasma using a multiplex PCR-NGS approach. Cell-free DNA was extracted from patient plasma (median, 9.4 ml; range, 2.9–10.2 ml) at a given time point and was used to detect ctDNA. A plasma sample was classified as ctDNA-positive if two or more tumor-specific variants out of the 16 were detected above a predefined threshold. The predefined threshold is based on Natera’s proprietary variant calling method, wherein detecting at least two out of 16 variants ensures optimal analytical performance of the assay, with greater than 95% sensitivity at a mean variant allele frequency of 0.01% and 99.7% specificity.32 ctDNA concentration was reported as mean tumor molecules per milliliter (MTM/mL) of plasma. Testing cadence was at the discretion of the treating physician, with results available in real time. Lead time was defined as the interval between the first ctDNA re-positivity after a documented negative result and the date of first clinical or radiographic evidence of recurrence.

Treatment and Response Assessment
All patients received curative-intent CRT, typically with DP-IMRT. Radiation dose was adapted to tumor size: <2 cm, 50 Gy; 2–4 cm, 54 Gy; >4 cm, 58 Gy, all delivered in 2-Gy fractions.6 Most patients received concurrent fluoropyrimidine-based chemotherapy, with or without mitomycin, unless clinically contraindicated.

Treatment response was assessed 12–16 weeks after CRT using physical examination (including digital rectal and inguinal lymph node exams), anoproctoscopy, and cross-sectional imaging (MRI, CT, or PET-CT). Clinical complete response (cCR) was defined as no detectable tumor locally, regionally, or distantly. For patients with an incomplete but improving primary tumor response, short-interval re-evaluation (within 4–8 weeks) was permitted. Recurrence was defined as local, regional, or distant disease. Locoregional failure was defined as recurrence at the primary site or in pelvic/inguinal regional nodes, with ‘combined local–nodal failure’ reserved for concurrent recurrence at both sites. Salvage management for locoregional recurrence was categorized as operative salvage (APR), nonoperative salvage (re-irradiation and/or systemic therapy), or best supportive care for patients medically ineligible for salvage therapy.

Phlebotomy Timeline
Peripheral blood was collected at physician-defined intervals throughout the treatment course (Supplementary Figure 3). Pre-treatment samples were obtained at any point before treatment initiation or within five days after starting CRT. During-treatment samples were collected more than five days after CRT initiation but at least seven days before its completion. End-of-treatment samples were drawn from seven days before through 42 days after the end-of-CRT. Samples collected more than 42 days after CRT completion were categorized as surveillance timepoints. Patients who re-converted from negative to positive ctDNA status during surveillance underwent ‘enhanced surveillance’, including directed clinical examination (digital rectal examination and, when appropriate, flexible sigmoidoscopy/anoscopy) and expedited cross-sectional imaging (MR pelvis, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, and/or PET-CT).

Study Endpoints
The primary endpoint was OS, defined as the time from ctDNA assessment to death from any cause or to last follow-up. Secondary endpoints included progression-free survival and the cumulative incidence of locoregional failure. PFS was defined as the time from ctDNA assessment to the first occurrence of local or regional failure, distant metastasis, or death. LRF was defined as persistent, progressive, or recurrent disease in the primary tumor or regional lymph nodes, with death and distant recurrence treated as competing-risks.

Statistical Analyses
Baseline characteristics were summarized using medians and interquartile ranges (IQR) for continuous variables, and frequencies with percentages for categorical variables. Univariate logistic regression was used to evaluate predictors of pre-treatment ctDNA positivity. Kaplan-Meier estimates were used to evaluate OS and PFS from the date of end-of-treatment ctDNA assessment, stratifying patients by time of clearance. Additional timepoint-specific Kaplan-Meier analyses were conducted for OS and PFS according to ctDNA status at each sampling point, measured from the corresponding ctDNA collection date. Survival differences were compared using log-rank tests. LRF was analyzed at the same timepoints using competing-risk regression, with cumulative incidence curves by Gray’s test.

Patients without a ctDNA result at a given time point were excluded from time point-specific survival analyses. If multiple samples existed in a given phase (e.g., during-treatment), the most recent test was selected. In surveillance, if all ctDNA results were negative, the most recent was used; if any were ctDNA-positive, the first positive test was selected. Analyses were performed in R (v4.4.0) using tidyverse (v2.0.0), gtsummary (v2.0.0), ggsurvfit (v1.1.0), ggalluvial (v0.12.5), and ggpubr (v0.6.0).
